issues.note: A heavy cardiology window (several NEJM outcome trials landed at once) but a light one for ED pharmacotherapy, with no ED drug RCTs. The EM picks are a toxicology guidance paper, a pediatric resuscitation dosing meta-analysis, a large nonrandomized ECPR study and a BP-target trial in prior stroke.
bottom_line: A suspected medical-aid-in-dying mixture exposure (benzodiazepine or barbiturate, opioid, plus digoxin, beta-blocker or TCA) needs a digoxin level, serial ECGs and poison center input. Have digoxin Fab, high-dose insulin and bicarbonate ready, and avoid flumazenil and reflexive naloxone in the mixed ingestion.

For pediatric resuscitation drug dosing, a habitus-corrected length tape (PAWPER) beat the Broselow tape on weight accuracy, dose accuracy and time to drug, while age-based weight formulas were consistently inaccurate.
Prehospital ECPR by helicopter teams was linked to doubled survival to discharge (40% vs 20%) in refractory OHCA patients 50 or younger, but the study wasn't randomized.

articles.takeaway: Accidental exposure to medical-aid-in-dying drug mixtures is survivable with fast, toxin-specific ED care
articles.title: Unintended Exposure to Medical Aid in Dying Drug Mixtures: Principles of Emergency Care.
articles.population: Narrative review with proposed management principles; US context as MAID expands (New York legalized it in Aug 2026)
articles.summary: MAID mixtures are self-administered at home and typically combine a benzodiazepine and/or barbiturate, an opioid, and a cardiotoxin such as digoxin, a beta-blocker or a TCA, so a child or other unintended person may ingest a partial dose. The authors propose early poison center contact, supportive resuscitation, activated charcoal or gastric aspiration when safe, a serum digoxin level and serial ECGs, and toxin-specific therapy: digoxin immune Fab, high-dose insulin for propranolol, and sodium bicarbonate for TCA-related QRS widening. They advise avoiding flumazenil and naloxone in these mixed ingestions. These are expert recommendations, not trial-based.
articles.why: A new exposure type for ED pharmacists to plan for as more states legalize MAID. Confirm digoxin Fab stock and a high-dose insulin protocol, and remember that reversing sedation can unmask seizures or arrhythmias in a mixed ingestion.

articles.takeaway: A habitus-corrected length tape beat the Broselow tape for pediatric resuscitation weight and dose accuracy
articles.title: Weight Estimation and Dose Calculation in Resuscitation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 250 studies of weight-estimation and dose-calculation tools in children (9 in children actually being resuscitated)
articles.summary: Compared with the Broselow tape, the PAWPER tape (a length-based tape that adds a body-habitus correction) was better for weight accuracy, dose accuracy and time to drug administration in every analysis. In paired comparisons it more than doubled the odds of an estimate within 10% of true weight (OR 2.48, 95% CI 2.04–3.02). Age-based formulas got fewer than half of estimates within 10%. No study reported patient outcomes, and children longer than the tape or with growth problems were often excluded.
articles.why: Weight errors are a leading source of pediatric code dosing mistakes. Supports habitus-adjusted tapes or measured weights over age formulas, paired with pharmacist-verified, pre-calculated dosing references.

articles.takeaway: Helicopter teams that could start ECPR on scene doubled survival to discharge in young refractory OHCA patients
articles.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.population: 231 adults aged 50 or younger with refractory OHCA, nationwide in the Netherlands (OnScene)
articles.summary: Patients attended by ECPR-equipped helicopter EMS teams (144) were compared with those attended by teams without ECPR capability (87). Survival to hospital discharge was 40% vs 20% (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.59–4.66), and favorable neurologic outcome at 6 months was 36% vs 13% (OR 4.22). Adverse events were more frequent with ECPR (32 vs 11). Allocation depended on which team responded, not randomization, so confounding remains possible.
articles.why: As ECPR moves earlier in the chain of survival, pharmacists will own the heparin bolus at cannulation, sedation and vasopressor plans, and post-arrest drug management. Worth knowing for EDs considering ECPR programs.

articles.takeaway: Targeting systolic BP under 120 after ischemic stroke or TIA cut major cardiovascular events by about a fifth
articles.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke.
articles.population: 4,368 adults with elevated BP and prior ischemic stroke or TIA, 30 sites in Brazil (OPTIMAL-STROKE)
articles.summary: In this open-label trial, achieved systolic BP was about 122 vs 135 mm Hg. Over a median of 3.9 years, cardiovascular death, MI, stroke or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure occurred in 10.9% with intensive treatment vs 13.5% with standard treatment (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.67–0.94). The composite kidney outcome was more common with intensive treatment, while overall serious adverse events were similar. A companion trial in type 2 diabetes (OPTIMAL-DIABETES, PMID 43001746) found no significant benefit of the same target (HR 0.90).
articles.why: Supports aggressive long-term BP goals once the acute stroke phase is over, which shapes discharge regimens and med counseling. It doesn't apply to acute BP management in the first hours of stroke, and kidney function needs monitoring.

articles.takeaway: Stopping primary-prevention statins in multimorbid adults 70 and older was noninferior at 2 years, but events ran higher
articles.title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease.
articles.population: 1,880 adults aged 70 or older (mean 77.5) with at least two chronic conditions taking statins for primary prevention, international (STREAM)
articles.summary: Participants were randomized to stop or continue statins and other lipid-lowering drugs in an open-label design. The difference in event-free survival time at 2 years was −2.0 weeks (95% CI −3.7 to −0.3), within the −5.2-week noninferiority margin. However, nonfatal MI, nonfatal ischemic stroke or death occurred in 12.7% after stopping vs 9.2% with continuation, and serious adverse events were 43.0% vs 39.8%. Follow-up was only about 2 years.
articles.why: Noninferior isn't the same as harmless: the raw event rates favored continuing. For pharmacists doing deprescribing reviews, stopping is a reasonable shared decision in frail older adults with limited life expectancy, not a default.

articles.takeaway: IL-6 blockade with ziltivekimab lowered inflammation markers but didn't reduce cardiovascular events
articles.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease.
articles.population: 6,376 adults with atherosclerotic CVD, CKD and hs-CRP of 2 mg/L or higher, multinational (ZEUS)
articles.summary: Monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab 15 mg cut free IL-6 by 76 and hs-CRP by 64 percentage points vs placebo at 24 months. Over a median of 33 months, cardiovascular death, MI or stroke occurred in 17.6% vs 17.7% (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88–1.11). Serious infections were somewhat more frequent with ziltivekimab (20.4% vs 17.9%). The trial was funded by Novo Nordisk.
articles.why: A major negative result for the inflammation hypothesis in cardiovascular disease, at least for IL-6 in CKD. Lowering a biomarker didn't translate into fewer events, and infection risk rose.

articles.takeaway: Pelacarsen cut lipoprotein(a) by about 70% but didn't reduce cardiovascular events over almost 5 years
articles.title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).
articles.population: 8,322 adults with established CVD and Lp(a) of 70 mg/dL or higher, international (Lp(a)HORIZON)
articles.summary: Monthly subcutaneous pelacarsen 80 mg lowered median Lp(a) from about 236 to 64 nmol/L at 12 months, while levels stayed near baseline with placebo. Over a median of 4.7 years, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 12.3% vs 12.1% (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90–1.15), with no benefit in patients with Lp(a) of 90 mg/dL or higher either. Serious adverse events were slightly lower with pelacarsen (37.3% vs 41.1%). The trial was funded by Novartis.
articles.why: The first Lp(a)-lowering outcomes trial was negative, which tempers expectations for the other Lp(a) agents in development. For now, high Lp(a) remains a risk marker that calls for aggressive LDL and BP control.

articles.takeaway: Vitamin A is recommended for confirmed measles, but no US liquid formulation makes it easy to give young children
articles.title: Clinical consultation: The role of vitamin A in the management of confirmed acute measles infection.
articles.population: Review of evidence and practical administration issues amid record 2026 US measles cases
articles.summary: US measles cases in 2026 are the highest in more than 30 years. WHO and the AAP recommend vitamin A for confirmed acute measles, but the US lacks an FDA-approved concentrated liquid, so children who can't swallow capsules need cumbersome extraction methods. The authors advise confirming the diagnosis, screening for drug interactions, and checking for toxicity symptoms in patients who already received vitamin A.
articles.why: Children with measles will show up in the ED. Pharmacists should know the age-based doses (50,000 IU under 6 months, 100,000 IU at 6–11 months, 200,000 IU at 12 months or older, daily for 2 days) and have a plan for preparing doses from capsules.

issues.note: A very quiet Sunday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue is shorter. The EM picks are two retrospective cohorts and a post hoc STEMI analysis, and the rest is a phase 2 trial, a small open-label RCT and pharmacist-practice data. Read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Nebulized TXA for hemoptysis didn't reduce 72-hour rebleeding in a matched ICU cohort, even as its use climbed to 78% of patients. It remains an unproven adjunct until randomized data arrive.

High bleeding risk alone doesn't identify STEMI patients who should skip aspirin at primary PCI: ischemic events ran numerically higher and bleeding numerically lower with prasugrel monotherapy, in both risk groups.
Don't start aspirin for sepsis on the strength of a large MIMIC-IV signal. The authors themselves say the lower early mortality can't be read as causal.

articles.takeaway: Nebulized TXA didn't reduce 72-hour hemoptysis recurrence in ICU patients who didn't need immediate embolization
articles.title: Analysis of tranexamic acid in hemoptysis: effectiveness in a noninterventional evaluation (ATHENE).
articles.population: 228 ICU adults with hemoptysis not needing embolization within 6 hours, 1 center, 2017–2021
articles.summary: A third of patients (75) got nebulized TXA, and its use grew from 0% to 78% over the study. After 1:2 propensity matching, recurrence of at least 50 mL by 72 hours was 10.7% with TXA vs 12.3% without (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.37–2.32), and 30-day recurrence, respiratory failure, embolization and length of stay didn't differ. Thirty-day mortality was higher with TXA (9.3% vs 1.9%; OR 5.9), but events were few and mostly tied to underlying malignancy. Patients bleeding more than 200 mL at admission were excluded.
articles.why: Nebulized TXA has spread faster than its evidence. It is low cost and reasonable to discuss, but it shouldn't delay airway protection, reversal of anticoagulation or embolization, and this cohort is too small to rule out either benefit or harm.

articles.takeaway: Low-dose aspirin in sepsis tracked with lower early mortality, but the authors caution against treating sepsis with it
articles.title: Time-dependent associations of documented low-dose aspirin administration with 28-day mortality and early safety outcomes in adults with sepsis: a MIMIC-IV cohort study.
articles.population: 31,888 adults with Sepsis-3 in a single-center US ICU database; 4,771 got aspirin 75–100 mg
articles.summary: Time-dependent Cox models linked documented enteral aspirin to lower in-hospital mortality during the first 24 hours (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31–0.75) and at 24–72 hours (HR 0.63), with no clear association after that. Restricting to patients whose SOFA qualified by time zero gave similar numbers but a less certain first-day estimate (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.28–1.03). A hemoglobin drop of 2 g/dL or more was slightly more common with early aspirin (RR 1.10), though many of those drops came before the first dose. The analysis had residual imbalance, and prior aspirin exposure was uncertain.
articles.why: Patients well enough to take enteral aspirin differ from those who can't, so survival bias is a real concern. A practical takeaway is narrower: don't reflexively stop home aspirin in septic patients without a bleeding reason.

articles.takeaway: High bleeding risk didn't identify STEMI patients who benefit from skipping aspirin at primary PCI
articles.title: High Bleeding Risk and Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary PCI in STEMI: A Post Hoc Analysis of the PREMIUM Trial.
articles.population: 2,189 Japanese STEMI patients randomized to low-dose prasugrel alone or aspirin plus prasugrel; 786 (36%) met ARC-HBR criteria
articles.summary: High-bleeding-risk patients had more 12-month death, stroke or MI (16.2% vs 6.2%) and more BARC 3 or 5 bleeding (10.9% vs 4.9%) than others. Monotherapy vs DAPT gave ischemic rates of 18.0% vs 14.5% in HBR patients (HR 1.29, 95% CI 0.91–1.82) and 7.4% vs 5.0% in non-HBR patients (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.01–2.37), with no significant interaction. Bleeding was numerically lower with monotherapy in both groups (HR 0.71 and 0.62). Precision was limited and the low-dose Japanese prasugrel regimen may not translate elsewhere.
articles.why: Keeps aspirin in the ED STEMI loading routine for now, even for patients at high bleeding risk. Bleeding risk matters more for later de-escalation decisions than for the first dose.

articles.takeaway: DOACs were linked to lower mortality and intracranial bleeding than warfarin for LV thrombus in high-bleeding-risk patients
articles.title: One-Year Comparative Outcomes of Direct Oral Anticoagulants Versus Warfarin In Patients With Left Ventricular Thrombus And High Bleeding Risks.
articles.population: 4,416 matched US adults with LV thrombus and high bleeding risk (2,208 per group), 2013–2023
articles.summary: At 1 year, DOAC use was associated with lower mortality (24.9% vs 29.3%; HR 0.84), systemic embolism (1.9% vs 3.1%; HR 0.58), intracranial hemorrhage (1.3% vs 2.3%; HR 0.56) and hospitalization (72.0% vs 75.5%; HR 0.89). Stroke or TIA, cerebral infarction and major bleeding didn't differ significantly, even though the abstract's conclusion mentions reduced major bleeding. These health-record data can't capture warfarin INR control or DOAC dose appropriateness.
articles.why: Adds support for off-label DOAC use in LV thrombus, which comes up with post-MI patients at ED discharge and on admission. Check renal function and dose carefully in this high-risk group, and note the reported results don't support a major-bleeding advantage.

articles.takeaway: One infusion of either factor XI antibody cut PICC-related clots by more than half, with no major bleeding
articles.title: Amrecibart and cenvacibart for the prevention of catheter-related thrombosis (ROXI-CATH): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
articles.population: 195 adults getting a PICC expected to stay at least 14 days, 12 centers in 6 countries
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to a single IV dose of amrecibart 300 mg, cenvacibart 250 mg or placebo, with ultrasounds at days 7 and 14. Venous thromboembolism by day 14 occurred in 20% with each antibody vs 43% with placebo (OR about 0.37 for both). There was no major bleeding in any group, and clinically relevant non-major bleeding was 3% in all three arms. Most clots were found by protocol ultrasound, the trial was industry funded (Regeneron), and it wasn't powered for clinical outcomes.
articles.why: Factor XI inhibition is moving closer to the clinic, and a single-dose agent would raise new questions about duration of effect and reversal. Good to have on the radar for patients with a PICC who present with bleeding or an arm clot in coming years.

articles.takeaway: More accepted pharmacist interventions were associated with better survival in a pediatric ICU
articles.title: Association of Cumulative Pharmacist Interventions and Interprofessional Adherence With Survival Among Patients Requiring Pharmacotherapeutic Optimization in a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Time-Dependent Cohort Study.
articles.population: 565 children with a PICU stay over 24 hours and at least one pharmacist intervention, 1 tertiary center, 2019–2021
articles.summary: Overall mortality was 11.9%, and the team accepted 72.2% of recommendations. Each additional cumulative intervention was tied to a small drop in the hazard of PICU death (HR 0.989, p = 0.040), and accepted interventions showed a somewhat stronger link (HR 0.983, p = 0.025), including in both surgical and non-surgical patients. Baseline illness severity remained the strongest predictor of death. Only patients who received an intervention were included, so there is no comparison to care without a pharmacist.
articles.why: Useful framing for justifying critical care and ED pharmacist positions: acceptance of recommendations, and not just their number, is what tracked with survival. The design can't prove causation.

articles.takeaway: A short dexamethasone course reduced nausea when starting oral morphine in opioid-naive cancer patients
articles.title: Prophylactic dexamethasone for prevention of opioid-induced nausea and vomiting in cancer patients: a randomised controlled trial (DEX-OINV Trial).
articles.population: 150 opioid-naive adults starting oral morphine, 1 tertiary cancer center
articles.summary: Patients got prophylactic oral dexamethasone (74) or no prophylaxis (76), with rescue antiemetics available in both arms. Mean nausea scores were lower with dexamethasone on day 1 (1.36 vs 2.93) and day 5 (0.74 vs 1.53), with a number needed to treat of 5 on day 1 for clinically meaningful nausea (adjusted OR 0.38). Vomiting fell on day 1 and no serious adverse events occurred. The open-label design and subjective outcome leave room for bias.
articles.why: A cheap option worth knowing for oncology patients started on opioids at ED discharge, but steroid effects on glucose and infection risk should be weighed. The result doesn't extend to non-cancer patients.

issues.note: A stronger window than most: one Lancet RCT in cardiogenic shock, three new intra-arterial tenecteplase trials and a small septic shock fluid RCT. The other picks are observational or meta-analytic, and the medetomidine item is a preprint that hasn't been peer reviewed.
bottom_line: Adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase took a hit: it didn't improve 90-day outcomes during thrombectomy (BRETIS-TNK2), and a basilar trial (INSIST-IT) stopped early for safety and lack of efficacy, with numerically more deaths.

In MI with cardiogenic shock, cangrelor reliably inhibited platelets where crushed ticagrelor mostly didn't, but it didn't prove non-inferior on 30-day clinical outcomes. Better platelet numbers haven't yet become better outcomes.

Medetomidine appeared in about 25% of Southern California fentanyl samples by August 2026, up from about 6% in May 2025. Naloxone won't reverse its sedation or bradycardia, so plan for it in overdoses that stay sedated.

articles.takeaway: In MI with cardiogenic shock, cangrelor beat crushed ticagrelor on platelet inhibition but missed non-inferiority on clinical outcomes
articles.title: Cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI): a randomised, double-blind trial.
articles.population: 605 adults with MI complicated by cardiogenic shock, 29 hospitals in 5 European countries
articles.summary: Patients got cangrelor (30 mcg/kg bolus, then 4 mcg/kg/min for at least 2 hours) or crushed ticagrelor 180 mg. In the roughly 20% of patients with platelet testing, a platelet reactivity index under 50% at the end of PCI was reached in 100% with cangrelor vs 22% with ticagrelor. Death, MI or ischemic stroke at 30 days occurred in 38% vs 41%, but non-inferiority wasn't shown against a very tight 1-point margin (difference −4 points, 90% CI −10 to 3). Major bleeding was 6% vs 5%.
articles.why: Gut absorption is unreliable in shock, so an IV P2Y12 inhibitor makes pharmacologic sense, but this trial doesn't prove it improves outcomes. If cangrelor is used, plan the oral transition: ticagrelor can be loaded during or right after the infusion, while clopidogrel or prasugrel must wait until it stops.

articles.takeaway: Limiting fluid boluses by bedside intolerance signals improved oxygenation in septic shock, but the trial stopped early at 35 patients
articles.title: Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial.
articles.population: 35 ventilated adults with fluid-responsive septic shock and high risk of fluid harm, 3 Chilean ICUs
articles.summary: Before each bolus, lung ultrasound, VExUS, E/e' and CVP were graded as green (500 mL), yellow (250 mL) or red (no fluid), compared with standard 500-mL boluses over a 6-hour window. The intervention arm got less protocol fluid (250 vs 650 mL), and PaO2:FiO2 rose by a median of 40.5 points vs a fall of 37.9 (between-group difference +78). Lactate and capillary refill changes didn't differ. Only 36 of 62 planned patients were enrolled, cumulative fluid was similar between groups, and the authors call the effect uncertain.
articles.why: A concept to watch rather than a protocol to adopt: fluid responsive doesn't mean fluid tolerant. It supports reassessing before every bolus in boarded septic shock patients and starting norepinephrine early rather than defaulting to more volume.

articles.takeaway: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy didn't improve 90-day function in large-vessel stroke
articles.title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke: the BRETIS-TNK2 trial.
articles.population: 380 patients with large-vessel occlusion eligible for thrombectomy within 24 hours, multicenter open-label trial
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy or thrombectomy alone. A modified Rankin Scale score of 0–2 at 90 days occurred in 40.0% with tenecteplase vs 46.8% with thrombectomy alone (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.50–1.14; P = 0.19). The numbers leaned against tenecteplase, though the difference wasn't significant.
articles.why: Tempers recent enthusiasm for routine IA lytics. Earlier digests covered benefit after thrombectomy in selected patients, while this trial tested giving it during the procedure. A separate phase 2 trial this window (RESCUE-TNK, PMID 42995180) improved reperfusion in medium-vessel occlusion (61% vs 28%), so patient selection may be the deciding factor.

articles.takeaway: Intra-arterial tenecteplase after basilar thrombectomy didn't help and the trial stopped early for safety and futility
articles.title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase for acute basilar artery occlusion with sufficient recanalization after thrombectomy: the INSIST-IT randomized clinical trial.
articles.population: 144 patients with basilar occlusion and successful reperfusion within 24 hours of onset, multicenter open-label trial
articles.summary: Independent ambulation (mRS 0–3) at 90 days occurred in 40.0% with adjunctive tenecteplase vs 50.0% with standard therapy (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.34–1.29). Symptomatic ICH was similar (6.2% vs 4.8%), but 90-day mortality was numerically higher (41.3% vs 26.5%; OR 1.96, 95% CI 0.97–4.03; P = 0.063). The safety monitoring committee recommended stopping for safety concerns and lack of efficacy.
articles.why: A caution against extending anterior-circulation IA lytic data to basilar occlusions. Pharmacists asked to prepare post-thrombectomy IA tenecteplase should confirm the indication and location rather than assume a class benefit.

articles.takeaway: TXA in severe pelvic fractures was linked to lower 24-hour mortality, but not to less massive transfusion
articles.title: Association of tranexamic acid with early death or massive transfusion after severe pelvic ring fractures: A nationwide registry-based cohort study.
articles.population: 5,288 adults with blunt severe pelvic ring fractures, Japan Trauma Data Bank, 2019–2023
articles.summary: With overlap weighting, death within 24 hours or massive transfusion occurred in 13.0% with TXA vs 18.1% without (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60–0.87). The result came from 24-hour mortality (RR 0.62), since massive transfusion alone didn't differ (RR 0.94) and any transfusion was more common with TXA. Timing of TXA wasn't available, and the association weakened when outcome time origins were aligned (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65–1.00).
articles.why: Doesn't change the CRASH-2 approach for bleeding trauma: TXA 1 g over 10 minutes within 3 hours, then 1 g over 8 hours. It does not establish a pelvic-specific benefit, so timing and early hemorrhage control still matter most.

articles.takeaway: Balanced fluids resolved DKA about 4 hours faster than saline, but lactated Ringer's carried hyperkalemia and AKI signals
articles.title: Effectiveness of various balanced electrolyte solutions in the resuscitation of patients with diabetic ketoacidosis: A pairwise meta-analysis and network meta-analysis.
articles.population: 18 studies comparing balanced solutions with saline; 16 studies in the network analysis
articles.summary: Compared with normal saline, balanced solutions shortened time to DKA resolution (mean difference −4.41 hours) and hospital stay (−0.43 days), with higher bicarbonate and lower chloride after resuscitation, though heterogeneity was significant. Lactated Ringer's (−2.60 hours) and Sterofundin (−4.30 hours) both shortened resolution vs saline. Hyperkalemia (OR 4.06) and AKI (OR 2.26) were more common with LR than saline, and comparisons between balanced fluids were indirect.
articles.why: Adds support for a balanced crystalloid in adult DKA. The LR safety signal comes from indirect, low-precision data, so keep following potassium closely while insulin runs. Sterofundin isn't marketed in the US, so Plasma-Lyte or LR are the practical options here.

articles.takeaway: Medetomidine rose to about a quarter of Southern California fentanyl samples within about 15 months
articles.title: Characterizing the Emergence of Medetomidine in Southern California Fentanyl Markets.
articles.population: Community drug-checking samples, Southern California, 2023–2026 (22 quantified; 13 tested for enantiomers)
articles.summary: Mass spectrometry of voluntarily submitted samples showed medetomidine co-present with fentanyl in about 6% of samples in May 2025, the month it was first detected, rising to about 25% by August 2026. Mean concentration was 0.4% by mass, often with lidocaine and xylazine. All 13 samples tested were racemic, which suggests the drug wasn't diverted from pharmaceutical dexmedetomidine. This preprint has not been peer reviewed, and drug-checking samples aren't a random sample of the supply.
articles.why: Medetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist, so expect sedation and bradycardia that outlast naloxone's effect, and possibly a severe withdrawal syndrome. Routine urine screens won't detect it, and medetomidine is now spreading beyond the eastern US.

articles.takeaway: Best available antibiotics within 24 hours cut 14-day mortality in MDR gram-negative bacteremia, mainly for 3GC-resistant organisms
articles.title: Early best available antibiotic therapy for multidrug-resistant gram-negative bloodstream infections: a target trial emulation.
articles.population: 1,412 adults with MDR gram-negative bloodstream infection, 19 Asian countries (ACORN-HAI), 2022–2025
articles.summary: Guideline-recommended therapy started within 24 hours of blood culture was associated with lower 14-day mortality (18.5% vs 25.6%; risk difference −7.1%, 95% CI −11.3 to −3.0). The benefit was clear for third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (−7.4%), and larger in severe infections. Estimates for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales and Acinetobacter were uncertain, and most of that therapy was polymyxin-based.
articles.why: Supports reviewing prior cultures and risk factors at the first ED dose, and using a carbapenem early when ESBL risk is high. Speed alone may not rescue carbapenem-resistant infections treated with polymyxins, where agent choice also matters.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window. The EM picks are a pharmacist-led stewardship study, two meta-analyses, a prospective analgesia cohort, a trauma tox study and a reversal-agent review, with two stewardship papers rounding it out. Read the observational items as practice context.
bottom_line: Intranasal opioids (fentanyl or similar) relieved acute pain as well as IV morphine at 20 and 30 minutes, with no extra adverse events, so you don't need to wait on an IV line to treat pain.
When ED pharmacists owned MRSA nasal PCR ordering for admitted pneumonia patients, anti-MRSA therapy dropped from about 6 hours to about 1 hour with no change in readmissions or mortality.
In trauma patients, most positive fentanyl screens reflected fentanyl the team had already given. Check the MAR before calling a urine drug screen evidence of pre-injury use.

articles.takeaway: Pharmacist-ordered MRSA nasal PCR in the ED cut anti-MRSA therapy for pneumonia from ~6 h to ~1 h
articles.title: Impact of MRSA nasal PCR in the emergency department on duration of vancomycin and linezolid for pneumonia.
articles.population: 200 adults with suspected pneumonia given anti-MRSA therapy in the ED and admitted, 1 US academic center
articles.summary: ED pharmacists took responsibility for ordering the MRSA nasal swab under an existing hospital protocol, and ED nurses collected it before the patient left the department. Median duration of vancomycin or linezolid fell from 5.9 hours before the change to 1.1 hours after it (p = 0.006). PCR ordering rose from 69% to 86%, which was not statistically significant, and length of stay, 30-day readmission and 30-day mortality didn't differ. It is a single-center pre-post design without a randomized control.
articles.why: A cheap, high-yield ED pharmacist task: order the nasal PCR with the first vancomycin dose so a negative result (NPV over 95% for MRSA pneumonia) can stop it before the patient reaches the floor.

articles.takeaway: Intranasal opioids matched IV morphine for acute moderate-to-severe pain at 20 and 30 minutes
articles.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Intranasal Opioids vs. Intravenous Morphine for Acute Moderate-to-Severe Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.population: 10 RCTs, 1,164 adults and children with acute pain in ED, prehospital, procedural or postoperative settings
articles.summary: Pain score reductions at 20 minutes (SMD −0.05) and 30 minutes (SMD −0.05) were essentially identical between intranasal opioids and IV morphine, with little heterogeneity. Rescue analgesia was also equal (RR 1.00). Overall adverse events, serious adverse events, respiratory events, hypotension, GI effects, dizziness and rhinorrhea didn't differ, and only altered taste was borderline more common with the intranasal route. The trials were small, so rare serious events can't be excluded.
articles.why: Supports intranasal fentanyl (often 1.5–2 mcg/kg, max about 100 mcg per dose, using a concentrated solution and an atomizer) as a first-line option for kids, fractures and patients without IV access. Split volumes above about 1 mL between nostrils.

articles.takeaway: Brivaracetam stopped status epilepticus in about half of patients as a second-line drug
articles.title: Brivaracetam for the termination of status epilepticus: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 10 observational studies of patients with status epilepticus given brivaracetam
articles.summary: The pooled response rate was 52% (95% CI 45–59%), with moderate heterogeneity. Studies differed in how many antiseizure drugs had failed first, how long seizures had lasted before brivaracetam, and the loading and maintenance doses used. Response looked better when brivaracetam was given within 24 hours at loading doses of about 200–300 mg. No comparative RCTs were available, so it can't yet be ranked against levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.
articles.why: Brivaracetam can be pushed IV quickly and has fewer behavioral effects than levetiracetam, but it costs more and lacks trial data. For now it is an alternative second-line agent, not a replacement for levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4,500 mg).

articles.takeaway: Idarucizumab remains the only dabigatran antidote, but its benefit rests on single-arm and observational data
articles.title: A safety profile on idarucizumab for dabigatran reversal: an update.
articles.population: Review of pharmacology, clinical and real-world evidence for idarucizumab
articles.summary: The authors summarize idarucizumab's pharmacology, the evidence behind it and practical points on giving it and caring for patients afterward. Its clinical benefit is supported only by the single-arm RE-VERSE AD trial and observational studies, with no comparator. They note that high cost and falling dabigatran use make routine stocking hard to justify in rural or resource-limited sites, that trial bleeding definitions don't map neatly onto real cases, and that follow-up care and anticoagulation stewardship after reversal deserve more attention.
articles.why: For dabigatran bleeds, give idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials). If it isn't stocked, 4F-PCC or hemodialysis are fallbacks. Plan when and how to restart anticoagulation once bleeding is controlled.

articles.takeaway: About 63% of positive fentanyl screens in trauma patients were linked to fentanyl the team had given
articles.title: Administered opioids and benzodiazepines and the interpretation of positive trauma urine drug screens.
articles.population: 1,420 trauma patients with a urine drug screen, 1 US Level II trauma center, 2023–2024
articles.summary: Fentanyl screens were positive in 70% of patients given fentanyl before urine collection vs 12.5% of those who weren't (aOR 15.3), and the result held when only prehospital doses were counted. Similar but smaller effects were seen for opiates (aOR 5.9) and benzodiazepines (aOR 6.1), while cocaine, cannabis and amphetamine screens weren't affected. Modeling estimated that 63% of fentanyl, 34% of opiate and 29% of benzodiazepine positives were associated with drugs given during care.
articles.why: Reconcile every positive screen against the EMS run sheet and MAR before it lands in the chart as substance use. Know which agents each immunoassay channel picks up (e.g., hydromorphone and oxycodone vary by assay).

articles.takeaway: Persistent pain at 2 weeks, not opioid use, predicted new chronic pain after ED discharge
articles.title: Early Post-Discharge Pain Persistence, Not Opioid Use, Is Associated with New-Onset Chronic Pain Among Opioid-Naive Emergency Department Patients: A Secondary Analysis of a Prospective Cohort.
articles.population: 483 opioid-naive adults discharged from 2 urban US EDs with a new opioid prescription for pain
articles.summary: At 6 months, 26.7% had developed new chronic pain (pain on more than half of days). Neck or back pain and longer pain before the ED visit predicted it. Pain that persisted at 2 weeks (OR 2.36) and moderate or severe pain at 2 weeks (OR 2.20) were associated with new chronic pain, while opioid use at 48 hours or 2 weeks was not. About 20% of the original cohort was lost to follow-up.
articles.why: The 2-week mark is a useful checkpoint: patients still in pain then need follow-up and a multimodal plan (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, PT), not more opioid refills. Keep ED opioid prescriptions short.

articles.takeaway: Extended-infusion pip-tazo may improve clinical cure in critically ill adults, but mortality benefit is unproven
articles.title: Prolonged Versus Intermittent Piperacillin-Tazobactam Infusion in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
articles.population: 7 RCTs, 6,080 critically ill adults (BLING III supplied most of the patients)
articles.summary: Prolonged (extended or continuous) infusion improved clinical cure (RR 1.23) across 6 small trials, but certainty was very low. The 90-day mortality estimate leaned toward benefit without reaching significance (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84–1.01), and BLING III carried 99% of the weight. Effects on 28-day mortality and antibiotic duration were uncertain. The authors conclude that the results fit the class-wide beta-lactam data but don't prove a pip-tazo-specific mortality benefit.
articles.why: Give the first pip-tazo dose in the ED as a 30-minute bolus so it isn't delayed, then switch to extended infusion (e.g., 4.5 g over 4 hours every 8 hours). Watch for Y-site incompatibilities when lines are crowded.

articles.takeaway: Turning off cross-reactivity alerts plus an allergy guideline raised beta-lactam use with no added reactions
articles.title: Impact of multimodal interventions on β-lactam use in patients with penicillin or cephalosporin allergy.
articles.population: 234 hospitalized adults with a documented penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, 1 US center
articles.summary: The intervention combined suppressing EHR beta-lactam cross-reactivity alerts, clinician education and a new beta-lactam allergy guideline. Penicillin or cephalosporin use rose from 65% to 81% (p = 0.006), and non-beta-lactam use fell from 27% to 14%. Allergic reactions, C. difficile infection, length of stay and stopping antibiotics for intolerance didn't differ. It is a small single-center pre-post study.
articles.why: Most penicillin-allergic ED patients can safely get cefazolin or a cephalosporin with a dissimilar side chain (e.g., ceftriaxone). Pharmacists can push the guideline and alert changes that make this the default.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window, so the EM picks are a large propensity-matched cohort, a systematic review and registry data. Two pharmacist-relevant AJHP studies and a JAMA newborn vitamin K cohort round it out.
bottom_line: For cannabinoid hyperemesis, reach for haloperidol or droperidol before ondansetron: either butyrophenone roughly halved 72-hour ED returns in a large matched cohort.

Rapid methadone titration (e.g., 30–40 mg start, +10 mg every 3–4 h to 50–80 mg on day 1) had no reported deaths in fentanyl-era or inpatient studies, which supports faster starts for ED-initiated or boarded OUD patients.
In children admitted with CAP, waiting past 4 hours for antibiotics didn't worsen outcomes, so stable kids can be observed rather than reflexively treated in the ED.

articles.takeaway: Haloperidol or droperidol cut 72-hour ED returns for cannabinoid hyperemesis by about half vs ondansetron
articles.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Haloperidol, Droperidol, and Ondansetron for Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome in the Emergency Department.
articles.population: Adult ED visits with a suspected CHS phenotype, TriNetX multicenter network, 2014–2024
articles.summary: Researchers made three propensity-matched pairwise comparisons of drugs given at the index ED visit. Return to the ED within 72 hours was lower with haloperidol than ondansetron (8.2% vs 15.1%; OR 0.50) and with droperidol than ondansetron (7.4% vs 14.0%; OR 0.49), while haloperidol and droperidol didn't differ (OR 0.75, not significant). In adjusted survival models, both butyrophenones independently predicted fewer returns and ondansetron did not, and coded adverse events were rare. It is retrospective, diagnosis-code based and lacks dose data.
articles.why: Supports putting haloperidol (often 2.5–5 mg IV/IM) or droperidol ahead of ondansetron on CHS order sets. Check a QTc and screen for other QT-prolonging drugs, and pair with counseling on cannabis cessation and topical capsaicin.

articles.takeaway: Rapid methadone titration protocols looked safe, with no deaths in fentanyl-era or inpatient studies
articles.title: Safety and effectiveness of rapid methadone titration protocols in opioid use disorder: A systematic review.
articles.population: 29 studies, 16,154 patients with OUD starting methadone, inpatient and outpatient settings
articles.summary: The most common protocol started at 30–40 mg and added 10 mg every 3–4 hours as needed, up to 50–80 mg on day 1, with day-7 doses of roughly 53–97 mg in the larger studies. Across the 18 fentanyl-era studies and the 18 inpatient studies that reported mortality, no deaths occurred; nearly all reported deaths came from two older case series built from coroner reports. Overdose was under 1% and sedation was usually mild. Heterogeneity prevented pooling, and overall evidence quality was low.
articles.why: Fentanyl tolerance makes slow 'start low, go slow' methadone starts leave patients in withdrawal for weeks. Pharmacists can help design monitored rapid-titration protocols for admitted or boarded OUD patients, with sedation checks before each extra dose and QTc review.

articles.takeaway: Major bleeding hit 3% of acute PE patients in 30 days and 13% after thrombolysis
articles.title: Major bleeding in patients with acute pulmonary embolism: results from the COPE study.
articles.population: 5,213 patients with acute PE, prospective multicenter Italian COPE study
articles.summary: ISTH major bleeding occurred in 3.1% within 30 days, split about evenly between early (under 7 days) and late events. Bleeding occurred in 12.9% of patients given thrombolysis vs 2.5% of those who weren't. Active cancer, prior bleeding, dementia, anemia, syncope and thrombolysis predicted early bleeding, while cancer, prior bleeding and anemia predicted late bleeding. Four clinical bleeding phenotypes predicted risk about as well as PE-SARD, BACS and VTE-Bleed.
articles.why: Puts a number on the lytic bleeding trade-off for ED PE decisions. Flag cancer, anemia and prior bleeding when choosing between systemic lytics, reduced-dose regimens or catheter-directed therapy, and keep reversal agents ready.

articles.takeaway: For children admitted with pneumonia, antibiotics within 4 hours didn't reduce escalation of care
articles.title: Time to antibiotics and outcomes for children hospitalized with community acquired pneumonia.
articles.population: 758 children (3 months to 18 years) admitted from the ED with suspected CAP, 4 US children's hospitals
articles.summary: About 59% got antibiotics within 4 hours of ED arrival. In inverse propensity-weighted models, escalation of care (more respiratory support, ICU transfer, vasopressors or a chest tube) didn't differ between early and later antibiotics (3% vs 2%; OR 1.46, wide CI). Length of stay, oxygen duration and cost also didn't differ. Events were few, so a small effect can't be excluded, and septic children aren't the target of this finding.
articles.why: Supports a period of observation for well-appearing children with possible viral pneumonia instead of reflexive ED antibiotics. When treatment is needed, amoxicillin or ampicillin remains the narrow-spectrum default.

articles.takeaway: Milrinone in pediatric fluid-refractory septic shock was linked to higher mortality and more cardiac arrests
articles.title: Fluid-Refractory Septic Shock in Children and Milrinone: Outcomes in a Two-Center, Retrospective Cohort in France, 2011-2021.
articles.population: 290 children with fluid-refractory septic shock on vasoactive drugs, 2 French PICUs
articles.summary: Milrinone was used in 16% of children, at a median of 0.5 mcg/kg/min. It was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR 2.57), more fluid boluses, more mechanical ventilation, more PICU cardiac arrests (48% vs 11%) and more adverse events. Milrinone was likely given to sicker children with cardiac dysfunction, so confounding by indication is a major limitation.
articles.why: Milrinone's vasodilation and long, renally cleared half-life can worsen hypotension in warm or vasoplegic shock. Reserve it for documented low cardiac output with adequate pressure, and favor epinephrine as the first inotrope.

articles.takeaway: AUC-guided vancomycin monitoring cut AKI risk by about a third vs trough-guided monitoring
articles.title: Still Chasing the Curve: Updated Evidence on Vancomycin AUC vs Trough Monitoring and Its Impact on AKI. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, 2020-2025.
articles.population: 80 studies, 27,067 patients; 30 direct comparisons (18,146 patients) published 2020–2025
articles.summary: In head-to-head studies, AUC-guided monitoring lowered AKI risk compared with trough-guided monitoring (RR 0.66), and the result held when restricted to KDIGO-defined AKI. Mortality (OR 0.83) and 30-day readmission (OR 0.95) didn't differ, though few studies reported them. Heterogeneity was moderate (I² 64%), and most included studies were observational.
articles.why: Reinforces the 2020 consensus guideline: start vancomycin from the ED with a weight-based load, then hand off to an AUC (400–600) Bayesian or two-level protocol rather than trough targets.

articles.takeaway: Starting an NSAID while on a GLP-1 RA didn't raise GI bleed or ulcer risk vs SGLT2i or DPP-4i
articles.title: NSAID initiation and risk for gastrointestinal bleeding in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.population: 68,881 veterans with type 2 diabetes starting an NSAID on a GLP-1 RA (13,433), SGLT2i or DPP-4i
articles.summary: One-year GI bleed or ulcer rates were about 1% in all three groups (0.9% with GLP-1 RAs). After adjustment, GLP-1 RA users had no higher risk than SGLT2i users (HR 0.85) or DPP-4i users (HR 0.82), and results were similar for GI bleeding alone. The population was mostly older men, and over-the-counter NSAID use wasn't captured.
articles.why: A common ED discharge question. A GLP-1 RA alone shouldn't stop a short NSAID course, but the usual GI risk factors (age, anticoagulants, prior ulcer, steroids) still call for a PPI or an alternative analgesic.

articles.takeaway: Newborn vitamin K refusal more than doubled to 6.8%, and refusers had over twice the intracranial bleeding risk
articles.title: Nonreceipt of Newborn Vitamin K and Risk of Bleeding.
articles.population: 5,240,780 infants born at 35–43 weeks, US hospitals in all 50 states, 2017–2025
articles.summary: Nonreceipt of intramuscular vitamin K rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who didn't get it had more bleeding by 6 months (288 vs 186 per 10,000; adjusted RR 1.47), more intracranial bleeding (33 vs 13 per 10,000; adjusted RR 2.43) and more deaths with bleeding during the birth stay (adjusted RR 2.69). Bleeding was identified from diagnosis codes, which may misclassify some events.
articles.why: Infants with late vitamin K deficiency bleeding present to the ED with lethargy, vomiting or seizures. Ask about vitamin K at birth, and know the treatment: IV or subcutaneous vitamin K 1 mg plus 4-factor PCC or FFP for life-threatening bleeds.

issues.note: A thin window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue leans on large observational ED datasets plus one systematic review and one NEJM trial. Read the cohorts as practice context rather than practice-changers.
bottom_line: Bystander naloxone works: when a layperson gave it before EMS arrived, EMS needed to give more naloxone less often and transported fewer patients. Keep handing out kits at ED discharge.
Nearly half of intoxicated ED patients had at least one electrolyte abnormality. If potassium is low, check magnesium and phosphate too, and replete magnesium before chasing potassium.
About 1 in 7 adults admitted from the ED with influenza still left without an antiviral. Start oseltamivir in the ED for every admitted flu patient, regardless of symptom duration.

articles.takeaway: Layperson naloxone before EMS arrival meant less repeat naloxone and fewer transports than first-responder naloxone
articles.title: Layperson naloxone administration and subsequent emergency medical services care for opioid overdose.
articles.population: 26,087 EMS activations for opioid overdose with naloxone given before EMS arrival, US national 2023 dataset
articles.summary: About 31% of patients got naloxone from a layperson and the rest from trained responders such as police or firefighters. After a layperson dose, EMS gave more naloxone less often (24.4% vs 34.8%; aOR 0.73) and transported fewer patients (79.4% vs 84.4%; aOR 0.78). Advanced airways (about 1.5%) and cardiac arrest (about 6%) were uncommon and similar between groups. The data are cross-sectional, so patient severity and refusals can't be fully separated.
articles.why: Supports ED naloxone kit distribution and take-home programs. Also a reminder that more patients may decline transport after bystander reversal, so long-acting opioid exposures can be missed.

articles.takeaway: In severe hyperkalemia (K 7.0 or higher), kidney function, not the potassium value, predicted urgent dialysis
articles.title: Severe Hyperkalemia in the Emergency Department: Factors Associated with Dialysis and Mortality.
articles.population: 378 non-dialysis adults with plasma K of 7.0 mmol/L or higher in the ED, 1 center, 2010–2024
articles.summary: About half of patients had an ECG abnormality and 28% had severe ECG changes, and higher potassium was tied to more ECG changes. Urgent dialysis was needed in 12.2% and was predicted by stage III AKI, stage V CKD and younger age, not by the admission potassium after adjustment. In-hospital mortality was 23% and tracked with older age, malignancy, female sex and MAP below 70 mmHg.
articles.why: Calcium, insulin with dextrose, and beta-agonists still come first, but this supports calling nephrology early for patients with advanced CKD or severe AKI rather than waiting on repeat potassium levels.

articles.takeaway: About half of ED ethanol intoxication visits had an electrolyte abnormality; low K flagged low Mg and phosphate
articles.title: Incidence of Electrolyte Abnormalities in Emergency Department Patients Presenting With Ethanol Intoxication.
articles.population: 223,456 VA ED visits (83,178 patients) with serum ethanol above 50 mg/dL, 2010–2019
articles.summary: At least one electrolyte abnormality was found in 48.8% of encounters, and 2.9% had a severe one. Hypokalemia roughly doubled to tripled the odds of hypomagnesemia (OR 2.64) and hypophosphatemia (OR 2.51). The population was 94% male veterans, which limits generalizability.
articles.why: Argues against skipping labs in clinically intoxicated patients. Pair a basic panel with Mg and phosphate when K is low, and add thiamine before glucose in malnourished patients.

articles.takeaway: About 86% of adults admitted with influenza got an antiviral in the ED, with gaps by region and demographics
articles.title: Changes in Antiviral Treatment for Hospitalized Adults with Influenza in United States Emergency Departments.
articles.population: 483,459 adults hospitalized from US EDs with influenza, 2016–2025
articles.summary: Overall, 86.3% received oseltamivir, peramivir, baloxavir or zanamivir in the ED, with a low of 72.7% in 2021 and 85.1% in 2025. Treatment was less likely in the West (OR 0.78) and South (OR 0.95) than in the Northeast, and differed by age, race, ethnicity and language. ED treatment rates rose and fell with national flu positivity (r = 0.59).
articles.why: Guidelines recommend antivirals for every hospitalized flu patient, even after 48 hours of symptoms. An ED pharmacist prompt or order-set default is an easy fix for the remaining gap.

articles.takeaway: Low-level pyuria drove a large share of unnecessary antibiotics for suspected pediatric UTI
articles.title: Low-Level Pyuria and Antibiotic Prescribing for Suspected Urinary Tract Infection in Children.
articles.population: 1,150 children (2 months to 17 years) with urinalysis at ED and urgent care visits, 4 Northern California sites, 2022–2023
articles.summary: Overall, 16.6% of children got empiric antibiotics. Low-level pyuria (trace leukocyte esterase or a few WBCs) raised the odds of starting antibiotics more than sixfold (aOR 6.62) compared with no pyuria. It accounted for about 17% of overtreatment in children whose cultures ruled out UTI, but only about 2% of appropriate treatment for confirmed UTI.
articles.why: Trace pyuria alone shouldn't trigger antibiotics. ED culture-callback programs run by pharmacists can stop unneeded courses once cultures come back negative.

articles.takeaway: Probenecid-boosted once-daily cefazolin performed like ceftriaxone for cellulitis needing IV therapy
articles.title: Addition of probenecid to beta-lactam antibiotics in the treatment of skin and soft tissue infections: a systematic review.
articles.population: 9 studies, more than 1,600 patients with SSTI
articles.summary: Most studies compared once-daily IV cefazolin plus oral probenecid with ceftriaxone or more frequent cefazolin. Treatment success, failure, relapse and admission rates were similar. Evidence for oral beta-lactams plus probenecid was thin but didn't suggest they were worse. Adverse events were reported inconsistently and were mostly GI, possibly more common with probenecid.
articles.why: A narrower-spectrum option for ED-to-outpatient IV cellulitis pathways (e.g., cefazolin 2 g plus probenecid 1 g daily). Check for renal impairment and drug interactions, such as methotrexate, before adding probenecid.

articles.takeaway: Dexmedetomidine caused hypotension or more vasopressor need in most ICU patients with RV dysfunction
articles.title: Safety of Dexmedetomidine Use in Adult ICU Patients With Right Ventricular Dysfunction.
articles.population: 245 ICU adults with echo-confirmed RV dysfunction given dexmedetomidine, 1 US center, 2017–2022
articles.summary: A composite adverse event (bradycardia, hypotension, higher vasopressor or inotrope needs, or asystole) occurred in 62.4% of patients after dexmedetomidine was started. Hypotension was the most common event, and about 20% needed more vasopressor support (mean rise of 0.06 mcg/kg/min norepinephrine equivalents). Event rates were similar across mild, moderate and severe RV dysfunction, and there was no comparison group.
articles.why: Relevant to boarded ED patients with PE, pulmonary hypertension or RV failure after intubation. Start low, skip the loading dose, and have a vasopressor ready if you choose dexmedetomidine.

articles.takeaway: Plozasiran cut triglycerides by about 80% and acute pancreatitis by nearly 80% in severe hypertriglyceridemia
articles.title: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis.
articles.population: 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia, SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 (multinational)
articles.summary: Patients were randomized 2:1 to subcutaneous plozasiran 25 mg or placebo every 3 months. At 12 months, median triglycerides fell 79–81% with plozasiran, about 45–47 percentage points more than placebo, and over 90% reached a level below 500 mg/dL vs about half on placebo. In pooled data, acute pancreatitis occurred at 1 vs 5 events per 100 patient-years (rate ratio 0.22). Adverse event rates were the same in both groups (73%).
articles.why: An APOC3-targeting siRNA given 4 times a year could prevent repeat hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis visits. Expect questions about it during ED med histories and discharge planning.

issues.note: Another light window with one ED drug RCT (topical TXA for epistaxis). The rest are meta-analyses, cohorts and a pharmacist-practice study, so read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Topical TXA applied directly to the bleeding site helped stop spontaneous nosebleeds that first aid didn't control. It's a cheap, low-dose ED adjunct, though it didn't clearly reduce 24-hour rebleeding.
ER guanfacine overdoses in teens cause near-universal bradycardia and hypotension. Supportive care with fluids, atropine as needed and cardiac monitoring was enough, and every patient recovered.
In ICU patients on carbapenems, doses above the renal-adjusted recommendation were tied to much more AKI. Re-check CrCl daily and adjust; don't leave the ED loading regimen running unchanged.

articles.takeaway: Topical TXA beat placebo for stopping refractory spontaneous nosebleeds in the ED, but didn't clearly cut rebleeding
articles.title: Effect of Topical Tranexamic Acid in Acute Spontaneous Epistaxis: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.population: 162 ED patients with spontaneous epistaxis not controlled by first aid (76 TXA, 86 placebo)
articles.summary: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, TXA was applied directly to the bleeding site. It achieved initial hemostasis in the ED more often than placebo (p = 0.047). Rebleeding within 24 hours was numerically lower but not significantly different (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.17–1.24), and significant rebleeding was rare in both groups (RR 1.50, wide CI). The trial was small and the result was borderline.
articles.why: Supports stocking a topical TXA option (often the IV 100 mg/mL solution on pledgets) for anterior epistaxis before packing. Pharmacists can standardize the concentration and how it's applied.

articles.takeaway: Pediatric ER guanfacine overdoses caused bradycardia and hypotension that responded to supportive care
articles.title: Extended-release guanfacine overdose in a pediatric emergency department: a systematic review and a 10-year retrospective chart review.
articles.population: 15 children at 1 tertiary pediatric ED over 10 years, plus 11 published pediatric cases
articles.summary: In the ED cohort (median age 14), 73% of ingestions were intentional, often in teens with psychiatric conditions. Nearly all patients had bradycardia and hypotension, and some had transient hypertension early on. Most got IV fluids (87%), 20% got atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, and 3 needed PICU care; none got naloxone and all recovered. In the published cases (mostly accidental ingestions in young children), naloxone had inconsistent effects.
articles.why: ER guanfacine is increasingly common in ADHD households. Expect delayed, prolonged alpha-2 effects from the extended-release form, and have atropine and fluids ready; naloxone is a low-yield adjunct at best.

articles.takeaway: Early tirofiban within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis improved 90-day outcomes in non-cardioembolic stroke
articles.title: Early antiplatelet therapy after intravenous thrombolysis in acute non-cardiogenic ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 4 studies, 1,394 patients with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke after IVT (2 RCTs: ASSET-IT, INSTANT)
articles.summary: In the two RCTs (1,191 patients), starting tirofiban within 24 hours of thrombolysis raised the odds of mRS 0–1 at 90 days compared with standard antiplatelet timing (OR 1.78). Symptomatic ICH (OR 1.19) and mortality (OR 0.84) didn't differ significantly, but the confidence interval for sICH was wide and events were few. Aspirin data came from only one small study.
articles.why: Current guidelines generally hold antiplatelets for 24 hours after lytics. If your stroke team starts using early tirofiban, pharmacists will need a dosing protocol and bleeding checks.

articles.takeaway: ED pharmacist medication review for complex chronic patients cut inappropriate prescribing by about 21%
articles.title: Transitional care from the emergency department: Impact of a comprehensive pharmacotherapy review in complex chronic patients.
articles.population: Complex chronic patients seen in the ED, 151 intervention and 151 control, 1 Spanish hospital
articles.summary: Pharmacists reconciled medications and did a full pharmacotherapy review within 24 hours of the ED visit (48 hours on weekends), sent reports to primary care at discharge, and followed up at 1 and 3 months. Compared with usual care, polypharmacy, anticholinergic burden, potentially inappropriate prescriptions and reconciliation errors all fell, with inappropriate prescribing down 20.6% (mostly drugs without an indication, benzodiazepines and antipsychotics). Physicians accepted 49% of recommendations, but healthcare use didn't change.
articles.why: Evidence for the ED pharmacist's role beyond resuscitation: med rec and deprescribing in frail, high-utilizer patients, with handoff to primary care.

articles.takeaway: Balanced fluids didn't beat normal saline for pediatric DKA resolution, length of stay or cerebral edema
articles.title: Fluid choice in pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 8 studies (RCTs and observational), 47,840 children with DKA
articles.summary: Among the RCTs, time to DKA resolution (MD 2.27 hours, not significant), hospital length of stay and PICU length of stay didn't differ between balanced electrolyte solutions and 0.9% saline. Cerebral edema and AKI risks also didn't differ, but those estimates came from very few events and had extremely wide confidence intervals. The authors conclude that the evidence can't show either fluid is better or safer.
articles.why: Either fluid is reasonable for pediatric DKA; follow your institution's protocol. This differs from the adult and pediatric sepsis data, where balanced fluids have a modest edge.

articles.takeaway: DOACs performed similarly to warfarin for recanalization and major bleeding in cerebral venous thrombosis
articles.title: Direct oral anticoagulants versus vitamin K antagonist-based standard care in cerebral venous thrombosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.population: 6 RCTs, 430 patients with cerebral venous thrombosis
articles.summary: Recanalization or radiological improvement at about 6 months didn't differ between DOACs and VKA-based care (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.81–1.09), and the result held after excluding a trial with weak randomization. Major bleeding was rare in both groups (2 of 188 with DOACs vs 4 of 190 with comparators; RR 0.60, wide CI). Trials were small and used different imaging outcomes.
articles.why: Supports transitioning CVT patients to a DOAC after initial heparin, which simplifies discharge. Avoid DOACs in antiphospholipid syndrome and pregnancy.

articles.takeaway: Continuous paralytics in ventilated sepsis patients didn't change mortality but lengthened ICU stay and raised VAP
articles.title: Impact of Neuromuscular Blocking Agents on Hospital Outcomes in Mechanically Ventilated Patients With Sepsis: Propensity Score Analyses of A Nationwide Sepsis Cohort.
articles.population: 1,255 ventilated adults with sepsis, 20 Korean hospitals (292 matched pairs)
articles.summary: About a quarter of patients got a continuous NMBA infusion within 3 days of ICU admission. In-hospital mortality didn't differ in either the weighted or the matched analysis (17.1% vs 18.8%). NMBA use was associated with ICU stays about 3 days longer and more ventilator-associated pneumonia (8.6% vs 4.5%), with trends toward longer ventilation. Residual confounding by severity is likely.
articles.why: Reinforces saving continuous paralysis for specific indications such as severe ARDS or ventilator dyssynchrony. For boarded ED patients after RSI, focus on adequate analgesia and sedation rather than routine paralytic drips.

articles.takeaway: Carbapenem doses above renal-adjusted recommendations were linked to much higher AKI risk in the ICU
articles.title: Carbapenem Renal Dose Discordance and Acute Kidney Injury in the Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.population: 490 ICU adults on carbapenems for 48 hours or more, 1 Vietnamese hospital
articles.summary: Sixteen percent of patients got at least 1 day of dosing above renal-adjusted recommendations based on Cockcroft-Gault CrCl. AKI occurred in 35.9% of those patients vs 4.4% with appropriate dosing (adjusted RR 8.1; 5.9 in matched pairs). The link with treatment failure didn't meet the corrected significance threshold. Reverse causation is possible, since AKI itself makes a fixed dose discordant.
articles.why: Makes the case for daily pharmacist renal dose review. Full doses for the first 24–48 hours of sepsis are still reasonable, but adjust once renal function is clearer.

issues.note: Another thin window: no ED drug RCTs were indexed, so this issue runs short (7 picks). The resuscitation items are a trial secondary analysis and a review, and the rest are observational, a trial protocol and pharmacovigilance data, so treat them as context rather than practice-changers.
bottom_line: At ED triage, older age, abnormal vitals, intentional ingestion and pesticides (especially paraquat) flagged the poisonings most likely to turn severe. Paraquat caused 60% of deaths.
Post-arrest temperature control: no subgroup of OHCA patients (by downtime or admission neuro exam) benefited from 33 °C over controlled normothermia, which supports fever prevention as the default.
In kids with severe drug anaphylaxis, antibiotics and NSAIDs dominate FAERS reports, and ceftriaxone was tied to the most deaths. Keep IM epinephrine ready when giving first doses in the ED.

articles.takeaway: Age, abnormal triage vitals, intentional ingestion and pesticides predicted severe poisoning; paraquat caused most deaths
articles.title: Prospective identification of risk factors for patients with severe acute poisoning in emergency departments in northern Taiwan.
articles.population: 2,470 ED patients with acute poisoning, 2 Taiwanese tertiary centers over 2 years
articles.summary: Prescription medications were the most common exposure category (32.5%), and ingestion was the main route. Severe poisoning (Poisoning Severity Score 3–4) occurred in 11.5%, and 3.1% died; paraquat accounted for about 60% of deaths, with warfarin, amphetamines, digoxin, benzodiazepines, CO and methotrexate among the other fatal agents. Older age, abnormal vital signs at triage, suicidal intent and pesticide ingestion independently predicted severe poisoning, and the findings held when vitals were removed from the model.
articles.why: Gives simple triage-level red flags for which overdoses need early tox consult and close monitoring. Several of the fatal agents (warfarin, digoxin, methotrexate) have specific antidotes the ED pharmacist should have ready: vitamin K/PCC, digoxin Fab and glucarpidase or leucovorin.

articles.takeaway: Pooled TTM and TTM2 data found no OHCA subgroup that benefited from 33 °C over normothermia
articles.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
articles.population: 2,789 adults after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, TTM and TTM2 trials (multinational)
articles.summary: The authors used machine-learning methods (causal forests and Bayesian trees) to look for patients who might benefit from hypothermia based on ischemia time, prehospital factors and the admission neuro exam. Six-month mortality was 49.4% with 33 °C vs 47.9% with controlled normothermia. Estimated individual treatment effects barely varied, and no subgroup showed a meaningful benefit for either 6-month mortality or poor functional outcome.
articles.why: Supports fever prevention rather than deep hypothermia as the default post-arrest strategy, which means less need for the heavy sedation, paralytics and shivering protocols that 33 °C requires.

articles.takeaway: ECPR patients clot and bleed at the same time, so anticoagulation needs individualized, frequently reassessed targets
articles.title: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients.
articles.population: Adults receiving extracorporeal CPR for refractory cardiac arrest (evidence review)
articles.summary: An international ECLS expert group reviewed how ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation, platelet dysfunction and the circuit itself push ECPR patients toward both thrombosis and major bleeding. High-quality evidence is scarce, and most practice is borrowed from other ECMO populations, so center-to-center variation is large. The authors argue against fixed anticoagulation targets and favor individualized dosing guided by repeated clinical and lab assessment.
articles.why: As more EDs launch ECPR programs, the pharmacist often owns the heparin bolus at cannulation and the infusion that follows. This review is a good primer on why one aPTT or anti-Xa target won't fit every patient.

articles.takeaway: Mayo's BLOOM trial is testing EHR-guided, individualized cefepime dosing in the first hours of sepsis
articles.title: Cefepime Dose Individualization in Early Sepsis: A Pragmatic Feasibility Trial Protocol.
articles.population: Target of 300 or more critically ill adults starting cefepime for sepsis, Mayo Clinic Rochester (cluster-randomized)
articles.summary: Standard cefepime dosing produces 10- to 30-fold variation in drug exposure in critical illness, and up to 70% of patients may have low levels early on. The BLOOM-1 trial uses a population PK model based on weight and eGFR from both creatinine and cystatin C, delivered through EHR decision support, and compares it with usual dosing. Patients with AKI, dialysis or ECMO are excluded, and the trial measures feasibility, fidelity and exploratory PK and clinical outcomes, with enrollment expected to finish in January 2027.
articles.why: Shows where empiric beta-lactam dosing is heading: model-informed doses that balance under-exposure against cefepime neurotoxicity. Ordering a cystatin C with the sepsis workup may become part of the ED pharmacist's dosing workflow.

articles.takeaway: Diagnostic uncertainty roughly doubled the odds of antibiotics for viral fevers in the pediatric ED
articles.title: Predictors of Antibiotic Overuse in Febrile Children: A Sub-analysis of the Prospective, Multicenter AutoPilot-Dx Study.
articles.population: 1,008 febrile children (90 days to 18 years) in pediatric EDs, multicenter Germany, Italy and Israel
articles.summary: Among 628 children whose illness was adjudicated as viral by panel testing, 186 (about 30%) still received antibiotics. Physician-reported diagnostic uncertainty (OR 2.09), nonexudative tonsillitis (OR 2.78) and rales (OR 1.82) independently predicted overuse. Having a diagnostic test result at presentation was not associated with less overuse.
articles.why: Stewardship in the ED is largely about reducing uncertainty at the moment of decision. Pharmacists can push for Centor or McIsaac scoring with strep testing before treating sore throats, and for watchful-waiting prescriptions.

articles.takeaway: Antibiotics and NSAIDs drove most pediatric severe anaphylaxis reports, and ceftriaxone was linked to the most deaths
articles.title: Drugs associated with severe anaphylaxis in children and adolescents: a real-word FAERS pharmacovigilance study.
articles.population: FAERS reports of severe anaphylaxis in patients under 18, 2004–2023
articles.summary: Disproportionality analysis using five signal-detection methods found 138 drugs with positive signals. Anti-infectives had the most reports overall (845), ibuprofen was the single most-reported drug (369 cases), and ceftriaxone was associated with the most deaths. Signals for IV immunoglobulin and sevoflurane were not reflected in their labeling, and outcomes were worse in younger children. As with all spontaneous-report data, these are signals, not incidence rates.
articles.why: Common ED drugs (ceftriaxone, ibuprofen) top the list. Observe first IV antibiotic doses in kids, have weight-based IM epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg) ready, and document the reaction clearly.

articles.takeaway: Statins plus interacting antibiotics (mainly macrolides) about doubled the odds of muscle toxicity
articles.title: Drug-drug interactions between statins and antibiotics: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
articles.population: 3 observational studies of statin users with or without interacting antibiotics
articles.summary: Pooling three observational studies, concurrent use of interacting antibiotics (largely CYP3A4-inhibiting macrolides) with statins was associated with a higher risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis (pooled OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.82–2.50). The estimate was stable in leave-one-out analysis, but with only three studies the analysis can't separate risk by statin or antibiotic.
articles.why: A common ED discharge pitfall: clarithromycin or erythromycin with simvastatin, lovastatin or atorvastatin. Choose azithromycin or doxycycline, or hold the statin for the course.

issues.note: A very thin weekend window: no ED drug RCTs and only one ED toxicology study, so this issue runs short (7 picks) and leans on sepsis diagnostics, shock staging and stewardship. Treat the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: About 1 in 6 adults with acute poisoning (mostly organophosphates) needed intubation, usually on arrival. Paraquat patients can deteriorate late, so keep watching them after a calm first look.
For propofol procedural sedation, adding esketamine 0.3 mg/kg (roughly 0.6 mg/kg racemic ketamine) gave opioid-level analgesia with far less hypoxemia than sufentanil.
Rapid diagnostics only help when someone acts on them: a direct call to microbiology at sepsis alert, or a BCID2 panel, sped de-escalation but didn't change mortality.

articles.takeaway: One in six ED poisoning patients needed intubation, mostly for organophosphates; paraquat failed late
articles.title: Incidence and Outcomes of Endotracheal Intubation in Patients Presenting With Acute Poisoning to the Emergency Department of a Tertiary Care Center in India: A Prospective Observational Study.
articles.population: 120 adults with acute poisoning, 1 Indian tertiary ED, followed 28 days
articles.summary: Most ingestions were intentional, with organophosphates the leading agent, followed by household corrosives. Intubation was needed in 15.8% (19 of 120), most often for low GCS and airway protection, then respiratory distress and heavy secretions. Most intubations happened at presentation, but paraquat patients tended to need delayed intubation as respiratory failure progressed. Overall 28-day mortality was 9.2%, higher among intubated patients and driven mainly by organophosphates and paraquat. The study is small, single-center and descriptive.
articles.why: For OP poisoning, early high-dose atropine titrated to dry secretions can head off some intubations. If you do intubate, avoid succinylcholine (cholinesterase inhibition prolongs paralysis) and limit supplemental oxygen in paraquat.

articles.takeaway: Esketamine 0.3 mg/kg with propofol balanced analgesia and safety, with less hypoxemia than sufentanil
articles.title: Comparison of the anaesthetic efficacy and safety of different doses of esketamine combined with propofol in hysteroscopic surgery: a randomised, double-blind controlled trial.
articles.population: 160 women (157 analyzed) having elective hysteroscopy under propofol TIVA, 1 Chinese center
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to esketamine 0.15, 0.3 or 0.5 mg/kg or sufentanil 0.1 mcg/kg, all with propofol 1.5 mg/kg induction plus infusion. Pain scores after recovery were lower with 0.3 mg/kg, 0.5 mg/kg and sufentanil than with 0.15 mg/kg. SpO2 below 90% occurred in 20.5% of the sufentanil group vs 0–5.3% of the esketamine groups. The lowest dose caused more intraoperative hypertension (22.5%), and the highest dose caused more emergence agitation (10%) and slower recovery. Propofol use didn't differ, and the trial was registered retrospectively.
articles.why: Supports a ketamine-propofol mix over opioid-propofol for ED procedural sedation when apnea risk matters. Remember that racemic ketamine needs about twice the esketamine dose.

articles.takeaway: An updated cardiogenic shock staging system uses SBP, lactate and number of vasoactive drugs or devices
articles.title: Updated Staging System to Define Cardiogenic Shock Severity A Cardiogenic Shock Working Group Report.
articles.population: 11,640 patients with heart failure or MI cardiogenic shock (CSWG registry, 2021–2025), validated in 1.4 million patients in a US health system
articles.summary: Mortality rose step by step with lower SBP (cutoffs 60 and 90 mmHg) and higher lactate (cutoffs 2, 5 and 10 mmol/L). The 2026 system counts vasoactive drugs plus temporary mechanical support devices to set stage (C: 1–2, D: 3–4, E: 5 or more). Compared with the 2022 criteria, 28% of stage D and 56% of stage E patients moved to a less severe stage, and those patients had lower mortality. Out-of-hospital arrest worked best as a modifier, while in-hospital arrest placed patients in stage E.
articles.why: Each added pressor or inotrope now moves the stage directly, so the ED pharmacist's drip count and lactate are part of the shock-team severity call.

articles.takeaway: Calling microbiology at sepsis alert doubled the odds of a 24-hour diagnosis and sped de-escalation
articles.title: Impact of early microbiology laboratory activation on rapid diagnosis and antimicrobial optimization in a sepsis alert pathway.
articles.population: 327 adults with sepsis alert activation, 1 Spanish tertiary hospital
articles.summary: Early microbiology lab activation meant the clinician phoned the on-call microbiologist when the sepsis alert fired, which happened in 65% of patients. A causative organism was identified within 24 hours in 59.6% of patients with activation vs 35.1% without (adjusted OR 2.99), and rapid diagnostic tests were used more often. De-escalation came a day sooner (median 3 vs 4 days). Days of therapy, ICU admission, length of stay and mortality didn't differ.
articles.why: A simple communication step pharmacists can build into ED sepsis pathways so that empiric broad-spectrum therapy gets narrowed sooner.

articles.takeaway: A BCID2 rapid blood culture panel improved day-1 antibiotic choices in ICU bacteremia but not survival
articles.title: Use of a molecular syndromic panel for the etiological diagnosis of bloodstream infections in critically ill patients: impact on clinical outcomes and antimicrobial use from a multicenter, prospective study.
articles.population: 126 critically ill adults with bloodstream infection, multicenter Italy (MULTI-SITA)
articles.summary: Adding the BioFire BCID2 panel to standard blood cultures wasn't associated with 30-day mortality (HR 0.97). By day 1, early de-escalation or a switch to appropriate therapy happened more often with the panel (55.6% vs 31.7%). Mortality was driven by SOFA score, concurrent infections and the causative organism. The sample was small and the study wasn't randomized.
articles.why: Panel results are only as useful as the stewardship response to them. Pharmacist review of BCID2 hits (e.g., resistance genes like CTX-M, KPC, mecA) is where the gain comes from.

articles.takeaway: Weekly face-to-face handshake stewardship rounds won over 80% acceptance and cut broad-spectrum use
articles.title: From policing to partnerships: Implementation of a handshake antimicrobial stewardship program.
articles.population: Hospital medicine and acute care surgery services, 1 US health system
