articles.summary: A pharmacist-physician co-led team rounded in person once a week with each partner service and reviewed every patient on systemic antimicrobials. Service-line champions handled scheduling and buy-in. After 1 year, more than 80% of recommendations were accepted on both services, broad-spectrum use fell, and prescribers contacted stewardship pharmacists more often and reported high satisfaction. The report is descriptive, with no control group.
articles.why: A practical template for extending stewardship to the ED or observation units, where relationships with prescribers matter as much as the recommendations.

articles.takeaway: Polymyxin B worked best at an AUC of 77–110 mg·h/L; higher exposure raised AKI risk
articles.title: Optimizing Polymyxin B Exposure in Carbapenem-Resistant Organism-Associated Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia: A Retrospective Observational Study.
articles.population: 138 patients with carbapenem-resistant HAP on IV polymyxin B with TDM, 1 Chinese center
articles.summary: Clinical success at 14 days was 45.7%, and most infections were carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter. An AUC below 77 mg·h/L independently predicted treatment failure (OR 0.33), while an AUC above 110 mg·h/L tripled AKI risk (OR 3.24). The median AUC was 77.5 mg·h/L, so about half the patients fell below the efficacy threshold. The study is retrospective and single-center.
articles.why: Supports AUC-guided polymyxin B dosing where TDM exists. It's also a reminder that newer agents (e.g., cefiderocol, sulbactam-durlobactam) are often preferred for CRAB when available.

issues.note: A thin weekend window with only one small ED RCT, so most picks are cohorts, case series and pooled case reports. Read them as practical pearls and hypothesis-generating, not practice-changing.
bottom_line: Half-dose alteplase (50 mg) for high-risk PE performed about as well as 100 mg in a small cohort, with numerically less major bleeding.
Methiodone (IC-26), a new methadone-derived designer opioid, causes a classic opioid toxidrome that responds to naloxone and may be missed on routine urine immunoassays.
In antidepressant overdoses, non-SSRI agents carried much more serotonin toxicity and symptoms than SSRIs; serotonin toxicity predicted ICU admission.

articles.takeaway: Low-dose (50 mg) alteplase for high-risk PE matched 100 mg on hemodynamic stability, with less ventilator time
articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of Low-Dose Versus Standard-Dose Alteplase to Treat High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism.
articles.population: 65 adults given alteplase for high-risk (massive) PE, 1 US academic center, 2011–2022
articles.summary: Patients were grouped by initial alteplase dose (50 mg vs 100 mg). Sustained hemodynamic stability at 24 hours was similar (32% vs 38%), as was in-hospital mortality (48% vs 45%). The low-dose group had fewer ventilator days (median 1.5 vs 6) and numerically less major bleeding (12% vs 25%, not significant). The cohort is small, retrospective and spans more than a decade.
articles.why: Supports keeping a 50 mg option in PE lytic order sets for patients at higher bleeding risk, though it isn't strong enough to replace the 100 mg standard.

articles.takeaway: Methiodone, a new methadone-derived designer opioid, caused severe naloxone-responsive overdoses needing ICU care
articles.title: Methiodone (IC-26) a case series: an old, but novel, opioid substance causing severe toxicity.
articles.population: 4 patients admitted to the ICU with confirmed methiodone poisoning, 2025
articles.summary: All 4 patients had respiratory depression, miosis and depressed consciousness, and all improved with naloxone. Plasma levels were 0.20–0.64 mg/L, and the estimated half-life in one patient was about 13 hours. Detection on routine immunoassays depended on the assay, and unlike methadone poisoning, no clinically important ECG changes were seen.
articles.why: A long half-life means recurrent sedation after naloxone wears off, so plan observation or a naloxone infusion. A negative urine drug screen doesn't exclude it.

articles.takeaway: Non-SSRI antidepressant overdoses caused far more serotonin toxicity than SSRI overdoses, even after adjusting for dose
articles.title: Clinical Severity and Serotonin Toxicity in Antidepressant Self-Poisoning: Implications for Clinical Risk Assessment.
articles.population: 168 ED patients with intentional antidepressant ingestion, single center
articles.summary: SSRIs made up 80% of ingestions. After adjusting for dose (in defined daily doses), non-SSRI exposures were more often symptomatic (56% vs 28%; aOR 3.4) and more often met Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity (24% vs 4%; aOR 8.2). Patients with serotonin toxicity were admitted to the ICU far more often (54% vs 10%). The non-SSRI subgroups were small and mixed.
articles.why: When triaging antidepressant overdoses, venlafaxine, TCAs and other non-SSRIs deserve closer monitoring, and early serotonin toxicity should prompt benzodiazepines and a cyproheptadine plan.

articles.takeaway: In DOAC bleeds and urgent procedures, guideline adherence was high, and PCC use led to very few clots
articles.title: Management of bleeding and nonelective invasive procedures in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs): a 5-year single-center observational study.
articles.population: 584 events (152 bleeds, 432 urgent procedures) in 547 adults on dabigatran, rivaroxaban or apixaban, 1 French center
articles.summary: All patients had DOAC levels drawn at the time of the event. Guideline compliance was 79% and wasn't linked to outcomes. Among 95 events treated with PCC, only 1 thrombotic event occurred. Drug levels didn't track with bleeding severity, but in bleeding patients on rivaroxaban, those with adverse outcomes had much higher levels (median 243 vs 88 ng/mL).
articles.why: Reassuring safety data for PCC in DOAC bleeds, and a reminder that a DOAC level (where available) adds more than timing of the last dose for urgent-procedure decisions.

articles.takeaway: For acute myofascial low back pain in the ED, trigger point injection beat dry needling and avoided rescue opioids
articles.title: Short-Term Pain Outcomes of Trigger Point Injection Versus Dry Needling for Acute Myofascial Low Back Pain in the Emergency Department: A Prospective Randomized Comparative Study.
articles.population: 52 ED patients with acute myofascial low back pain (49 analyzed), single center
articles.summary: Pain dropped by 87% at 30 minutes after trigger point injection vs 33% after dry needling (difference 54 percentage points). Injection patients had lower pain at every time point, and none needed rescue IV fentanyl, compared with 65% after dry needling. No procedure complications occurred. The trial was small, unblinded and only followed patients for an hour.
articles.why: Supports trigger point injection (usually a local anesthetic) as an opioid-sparing ED option for back pain. Pharmacists can help standardize agent, volume and max local anesthetic dose.

articles.takeaway: In pediatric septic shock, balanced crystalloids cut hyperchloremia and dialysis but not mortality or AKI
articles.title: Balanced Crystalloids Versus Normal Saline for Fluid Resuscitation in Pediatric Septic Shock: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 9 studies (5 RCTs including PRoMPT BOLUS), children with sepsis or septic shock
articles.summary: Balanced fluids didn't significantly lower mortality (RR 0.94) or AKI (RR 0.84), and trial sequential analysis showed the evidence is still underpowered. They did reduce renal replacement therapy (RR 0.74) and hyperchloremia (RR 0.65). MAKE30, ventilation and length of stay didn't differ.
articles.why: Supports defaulting to LR or Plasma-Lyte for pediatric sepsis boluses, with the honest caveat that mortality benefit isn't proven.

articles.takeaway: A recent negative rectal swab nearly ruled out Pseudomonas and MDR gram-negative bacteremia in febrile neutropenia
articles.title: Challenging the Dogma: Can Rectal Colonization Status Guide Narrow-Spectrum Empiric Antibiotic Therapy in Febrile Neutropenia?
articles.population: 577 high-risk febrile neutropenia episodes in 415 patients with hematologic cancers, 1 Spanish center
articles.summary: Bloodstream infections occurred in 14% of episodes. A rectal swab within 7 days had a negative predictive value of 99.3% for Pseudomonas bacteremia and 98.1% for other MDR gram-negative bacteremia. Among 251 episodes with a negative swab, only 1 had Pseudomonas bacteremia. Overall BSI rates were low, which limits generalizability.
articles.why: Hypothesis-generating support for colonization-guided de-escalation. For now, keep cefepime or pip-tazo as the ED default for febrile neutropenia.

articles.takeaway: Adding rifampin or phenytoin sped recovery from Paxlovid-induced tacrolimus toxicity
articles.title: Drug Rescue for Paxlovid-Induced Tacrolimus Toxicity: A Pooled Analysis of Case Reports.
articles.population: 52 patients (51 published plus 1 new case) with tacrolimus toxicity after nirmatrelvir-ritonavir
articles.summary: Patients given a CYP3A4 inducer (rifampin or phenytoin) had tacrolimus levels normalize faster than those managed by stopping the drug alone (median 4 vs 6 days), and creatinine recovered faster (3 vs 7 days). After adjustment, inducer rescue shortened recovery by 2.6 days for tacrolimus and 4 days for creatinine. No serious adverse events were reported, but pooled case reports carry heavy selection bias.
articles.why: Transplant patients on Paxlovid can show up in the ED with AKI and toxic tacrolimus levels. Know this rescue option, and coordinate with transplant before adding an inducer.

issues.note: Covers articles indexed since yesterday's run. One ED drug RCT (renal colic) plus a few useful tox and stroke papers; the rest are meta-analyses and cohorts, so read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: For renal colic, an IV NSAID beats IV acetaminophen as the opioid-free first choice; acetaminophen needed the most rescue fentanyl.
Don't trust xylazine test strips on urine. They missed about 3 of 4 xylazine-positive samples from fentanyl patients.
In overdose patients, malignant ventricular dysrhythmias are rare (0.06%). Most cardiac trouble is hypotension or bradycardia from clonidine, beta-blockers or CCBs.

articles.takeaway: For ED renal colic, IV dexketoprofen and ibuprofen edged out IV acetaminophen, with less rescue fentanyl
articles.title: Opioid-free analgesia for acute renal colic: a randomized, double-blind, head-to-head comparison of intravenous ibuprofen, dexketoprofen trometamol and paracetamol in the emergency department.
articles.population: 251 adults with acute renal colic, 1 ED (single-center)
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to IV ibuprofen 400 mg, dexketoprofen 50 mg or acetaminophen 1 g over 15 minutes. The primary outcome, at least a 50% pain drop at 30 minutes, didn't differ significantly (77%, 74% and 66%). After adjusting for baseline pain, dexketoprofen gave lower 30-minute pain scores than acetaminophen (by 9.5 mm on a 100-mm scale) and lower odds of needing rescue fentanyl (OR 0.40). Mild side effects were rare and similar across groups, but the trial wasn't registered.
articles.why: Supports an IV NSAID (ketorolac or ibuprofen in the US, since dexketoprofen isn't available) as the first renal colic order, with acetaminophen as the backup when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

articles.takeaway: About 1 in 20 poisonings had cardiac complications, almost all hypotension or bradycardia; ventricular dysrhythmias were very rare
articles.title: Cardiac toxicity and dysrhythmias in acute poisoning: a ten-year cohort study.
articles.population: 9,743 acute poisoning presentations managed by a specialist toxicology service over 10 years
articles.summary: Cardiac complications occurred in 4.9% of presentations: hypotension in 3.8% and primary dysrhythmias in 1.7%. Most dysrhythmias were isolated bradycardia, mainly from clonidine (40%) and beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker poisoning (35%). Only 6 patients (0.06%) had ventricular dysrhythmias, linked to sotalol, methadone, escitalopram and tricyclics, and none of the 21 deaths was attributed to a poisoning-related dysrhythmia.
articles.why: Helps decide who needs prolonged telemetry. Focus monitoring on QT-prolonging and sodium-channel-blocking ingestions, and keep atropine, calcium and high-dose insulin ready for BB/CCB cases.

articles.takeaway: Xylazine test strips on urine missed most xylazine exposures in fentanyl-positive patients
articles.title: Diagnostic performance of xylazine test strips in urine from fentanyl-positive hospitalized patients.
articles.population: 250 residual urine samples from fentanyl-positive hospitalized patients, 1 US center
articles.summary: LC-MS found xylazine in 28% of samples. Compared with LC-MS, the commercial strips had 27% sensitivity and 78% specificity, with likelihood ratios near 1 (positive 1.2, negative 0.94). Over 90% of positive samples had xylazine levels below the strip's 1,000 ng/mL detection threshold.
articles.why: These strips were built for drug checking, not urine. Assume xylazine in fentanyl overdoses with prolonged sedation or wounds, and don't rule it out based on a negative strip.

articles.takeaway: Thrombolytics in pregnancy showed no extra maternal bleeding risk, though fetal loss was somewhat higher
articles.title: Maternal and Fetal Safety Outcomes of Thrombolytics for Ischemic Stroke in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Aggregated Case Series.
articles.population: 216 pregnant patients given thrombolytics (85 for ischemic stroke), 123 published studies
articles.summary: Symptomatic ICH rates were similar to those in young nonpregnant stroke patients given lytics. Miscarriage (12.4 percentage points higher) and stillbirth (5.9 points higher) were more common than in the general pregnant population. However, only 6 of 32 fetal deaths were judged likely caused by the thrombolytic. Case reports are prone to publication bias, and the underlying disease was hard to separate from drug effects.
articles.why: Pregnancy alone shouldn't rule out alteplase or tenecteplase for a disabling stroke. Useful when a stroke code involves a pregnant patient and the team asks about lytic safety.

articles.takeaway: Across TBI drug trials, TXA had the clearest mortality signal, mostly driven by CRASH-3
articles.title: Comparative effectiveness and safety of pharmacological interventions for secondary brain injury in adult traumatic brain injury: a network meta-analysis of randomized trials.
articles.population: 34 RCTs, 23,165 adults with TBI
articles.summary: TXA was associated with lower mortality (OR 0.90), as was erythropoietin (OR 0.64, from only 2 heterogeneous trials). Neither TXA nor hypertonic saline improved functional outcome, and the large statin effect came from 2 small trials with very low certainty. TXA wasn't linked to more thromboembolism or AKI.
articles.why: Reinforces early TXA (1 g within 3 hours) for TBI patients with mild to moderate injury and doesn't support routine statins, progesterone or other neuroprotectants.

articles.takeaway: Corticosteroids in septic shock modestly cut 28-day mortality and sped shock reversal
articles.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Corticosteroids vs. No Corticosteroids in Septic Shock Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 11 RCTs, 6,332 adults with septic shock
articles.summary: Steroids reduced 28-day mortality (RR 0.91), or about 27 fewer deaths per 1,000 patients, with no heterogeneity. Shock reversed about 1.25 days sooner, while ICU length of stay didn't differ significantly. Hyperglycemia was more common with steroids in every trial, and certainty was rated moderate for mortality.
articles.why: Supports hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for patients on escalating norepinephrine. Plan glucose monitoring and insulin when steroids start.

articles.takeaway: Dosing heparin infusions by adjusted body weight cut supratherapeutic aPTTs in heavier patients
articles.title: Anticoagulation stewardship quality improvement project to decrease incidence of supratherapeutic activated partial thromboplastic time in overweight cancer patients on unfractionated heparin infusions.
articles.population: Hospitalized cancer patients on high-intensity UFH with weight over 130% of IBW and BMI 40 or less, 1 US center
articles.summary: The protocol switched initial UFH dosing from actual to adjusted body weight in this group. With a bolus, first supratherapeutic aPTTs fell by 37% (RR 0.63) and first therapeutic aPTTs rose (RR 1.82). Without a bolus, supratherapeutic aPTTs fell by 39% (RR 0.61), and time to therapeutic range was shorter after the change.
articles.why: Relevant to ED heparin starts for PE and ACS. Pharmacists can push for an adjusted-weight trigger based on percent of IBW rather than a BMI-40 cutoff alone.

articles.takeaway: More than a quarter of US adults said they had exaggerated or invented symptoms to get antibiotics
articles.title: Symptom Misrepresentation to Obtain Antibiotics.
articles.population: 959 US adults, national online nonprobability sample
articles.summary: In total, 27.9% reported misrepresenting symptoms to get antibiotics, most often for cold-like illness, and about half of them both exaggerated and fabricated symptoms. Common reasons were feeling very sick, believing antibiotics work, and needing to return to work or other responsibilities. Younger age, feeling dismissed by clinicians, and believing antibiotic resistance is a hoax were the strongest predictors.
articles.why: Explains some of the pressure behind ED and urgent care URI prescribing. Symptomatic treatment plans and validating patients' concerns may work better than simply saying no.

issues.note: Covers articles indexed since yesterday's run. No big ED drug RCTs this window, so most picks are cohorts and trial secondary analyses; read the observational items as hypothesis-generating.
bottom_line: Patients discharged after stimulant toxicity have meaningful 1-year mortality, mostly from opioid-involved overdose. Offer naloxone at discharge even when the visit was for meth or cocaine.
Nebulized TXA for stable post-tonsillectomy bleeding with a small clot sharply cut the need for surgery in kids. It's a cheap, low-risk ED option worth a protocol.
Intra-arterial tenecteplase after thrombectomy helped mainly when reperfusion was incomplete (eTICI 2b50–67), not after near-complete reperfusion.

articles.takeaway: About 2% of patients died within a year of an ED visit for stimulant toxicity, mostly from opioid-involved overdoses
articles.title: One-year mortality following emergency department visits for stimulant toxicity.
articles.population: 2,356 patients discharged from the ED with stimulant toxicity, US statewide linked database
articles.summary: Linked ED, hospital and death records showed 1-year all-cause mortality of 2.1% after ED discharge for stimulant toxicity. Those who died were young (median age 35) and died a median of 118 days after the visit. Two-thirds of deaths were overdoses, and opioids were involved in 54% of them. A reference cohort of opioid-toxicity visits had higher 1-year mortality (6.9%).
articles.why: Supports giving naloxone and harm-reduction counseling to stimulant patients at ED discharge, since the fentanyl supply drives much of their later risk.

articles.takeaway: In witnessed pediatric OHCA, earlier epinephrine wasn't clearly linked to better 1-month survival
articles.title: Timing of the Adrenaline Administration in Witnessed Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Retrospective, National Cohort Study in Japan, Using a 2014-2020 Dataset.
articles.population: 259 children with witnessed OHCA who received epinephrine, Japanese national registry (JAAM-OHCA)
articles.summary: The authors used time-dependent propensity score risk-set matching to reduce resuscitation time bias, comparing children given epinephrine in each time window with children not yet given it. None of the time windows (1–10 up to 26–30 minutes after EMS contact) showed a significant difference in 1-month survival or favorable neurologic outcome. Confidence intervals were very wide (e.g., RR 2.94, 95% CI 0.38–22.8 for 1–10 minutes), so the study was underpowered to detect a real effect.
articles.why: A null result from a small sample doesn't overturn the push for early epinephrine in pediatric arrest. Keep weight-based doses ready, and read this as a lack of power rather than proof of no benefit.

articles.takeaway: Adjunctive cenobamate ended most refractory focal status epilepticus cases in a real-world cohort
articles.title: Cenobamate in Focal-Onset Refractory and Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus: A Multicenter Cohort Study With Matched Analysis.
articles.population: 31 adults with focal refractory or super-refractory SE, multicenter registry (Spain), plus 56 matched controls
articles.summary: Cenobamate was started a median of 4 days into SE, after 5 failed antiseizure meds, at a median of 50 mg/day enterally. SE resolved in 84% (all RSE patients and 64% of SRSE), with response at a median of 2 days. In the propensity-matched comparison, resolution was more common with cenobamate (82% vs 57%; aOR 5.9). No serious drug-related adverse events occurred, and somnolence was the most common mild effect.
articles.why: Cenobamate is enteral-only and slow to titrate, so it's a late ICU add-on rather than an ED option. Watch for its interactions (it raises phenytoin and phenobarbital levels and lowers lamotrigine levels).

articles.takeaway: Intra-arterial tenecteplase after thrombectomy helped only when reperfusion was incomplete
articles.title: Relationship Between the eTICI Score Before Randomization and 90-Day Outcome: A Post Hoc Analysis of ANGEL-TNK Trial.
articles.population: 253 patients with anterior-circulation LVO after successful EVT, multicenter China (ANGEL-TNK)
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to intra-arterial tenecteplase 0.125 mg/kg or standard care after eTICI 2b50 or better reperfusion. With partial reperfusion (eTICI 2b50–67), tenecteplase more than doubled the rate of mRS 0–1 at 90 days (44.8% vs 19.5%; RR 2.08). With near-complete reperfusion (eTICI 2c–3), it gave no benefit and raised any ICH within 48 hours (33.3% vs 20.0%), though symptomatic ICH and death didn't differ.
articles.why: Helps answer which post-EVT patients should get IA lytic. Expect neuro-IR to ask about TNK dosing for patients with residual distal occlusion.

articles.takeaway: IV N-acetylcysteine was linked to lower 21-day mortality in acute liver failure not caused by acetaminophen
articles.title: Evaluation of the Association of N-Acetylcysteine and Mortality in Non-Acetaminophen-Induced Acute Liver Failure.
articles.population: 200 adults with non-acetaminophen acute liver failure (85 got IV NAC), single US center
articles.summary: After inverse probability weighting for severity, comorbidities and etiology, IV NAC was associated with lower in-hospital mortality at 21 days (48.9% vs 62.1%; OR 0.59). Time to INR and LFT normalization and length of stay didn't differ. The study is retrospective and single-center, so unmeasured confounding remains possible.
articles.why: Supports starting the IV NAC protocol early in non-APAP ALF, for example from drugs, herbals or mushrooms, while transplant is being considered. Its low risk favors giving it when the etiology is unclear.

articles.takeaway: Nebulized TXA cut surgery for pediatric post-tonsillectomy bleeding, especially with small clots
articles.title: Nebulized Tranexamic Acid in Posttonsillectomy Hemorrhage: A Retrospective Study of a Standardized Treatment Algorithm.
articles.population: 121 children presenting to the ED with post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage, 1 US tertiary children's hospital
articles.summary: Starting in March 2024, stable children got nebulized TXA and were then triaged by clot size. Overall surgery rates were 66% with TXA vs 80% before the protocol (not significant). Among children with small clots (under 50% of the fossa), surgery dropped from 88% to 21%. No TXA adverse events were reported, and the authors estimated 32 surgeries avoided and about $138,000 saved.
articles.why: An easy order set item for the ED, usually the IV TXA solution given by nebulizer. Pharmacists can standardize the dose and concentration.

articles.takeaway: After DAPT, clopidogrel beat aspirin monotherapy in higher-risk PCI patients without more bleeding
articles.title: Clopidogrel Versus Aspirin Monotherapy According to Atherothrombotic Risk Profile.
articles.population: 5,506 post-PCI patients after completing DAPT, SMART-CHOICE 3 trial (South Korea)
articles.summary: Patients were grouped by TIMI secondary-prevention risk score and PCI complexity. In the higher-risk group (82% of patients), clopidogrel reduced death, MI or stroke compared with aspirin (4.6% vs 7.4%; HR 0.67) over a median of 2.3 years. Lower-risk patients showed no difference, and the interaction test wasn't significant. Bleeding was similar across groups.
articles.why: Adds weight to clopidogrel as long-term single antiplatelet therapy after PCI. Remember CYP2C19 poor metabolizers and the PPI interaction (avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole).

articles.takeaway: A third of children delabeled from penicillin allergy still never received penicillin again
articles.title: Beyond delabeling: long-term penicillin use and avoidance following negative penicillin challenge in children.
articles.population: 305 children referred for penicillin allergy evaluation, 1 Israeli pediatric allergy clinic
articles.summary: Most children had a direct oral challenge (94%), and 98.6% tolerated it. Full tolerance, including a 5-day home course, was confirmed in 80%. Among tolerant children with follow-up, 64% later used penicillin again with no reactions, while 36% had no documented use. Younger age and less time since the challenge predicted reuse.
articles.why: Delabeling only works if the EHR allergy entry is actually removed. ED pharmacists can check for a negative challenge and remove stale labels before defaulting to broader agents.
